pages.x: Toyotomi Hideyoshi, born a peasant, had finished uniting Japan after a century of civil war. With hundreds of thousands of battle-hardened samurai and nothing left to conquer at home, he set out to conquer Ming China, and asked Korea to let his armies through. Korea refused.
In May 1592 some 150,000 Japanese troops landed at Busan. Armed with muskets, they swept north, took Seoul in under three weeks and soon held Pyongyang. King Seonjo fled toward the Chinese border.

At sea it was another story. Admiral Yi Sun-sin led a fleet that included turtle ships, low warships roofed with iron spikes, with cannon on every side and a dragon head that belched smoke. He won battle after battle and cut the sea lanes that fed the Japanese armies.

The Ming emperor Wanli sent a great army to help Korea, and in 1593 it took back Pyongyang. Korean volunteer armies, monks among them, fought behind the Japanese lines. The war sank into years of talks that went nowhere.

When the war began again in 1597, Yi, dismissed and jailed through court jealousy, was called back with only 13 ships. In the narrow strait of Myeongnyang he beat a Japanese fleet of more than 100 by using the fierce tidal current against it.

Hideyoshi's soldiers were rewarded for proof of their kills, and sent home the noses and ears of tens of thousands of Koreans, soldiers and civilians. They lie buried in the Mimizuka, the Ear Mound, in Kyoto.

pages.x: Hideyoshi died in 1598, and the Japanese pulled out. In the last battle, at Noryang, Yi Sun-sin was struck by a bullet. He told his men to hide his death until the battle was won.
The war wrecked Korea, emptied the Ming treasury and ended Japan's hopes of a mainland empire for 300 years. Yi Sun-sin is Korea's greatest hero, and his statue stands in the heart of Seoul.
pts: Korea and Ming China drove Japan out
